newsitem.title: USA: Quaker Oats profit reverses loss despite weak Snapple.
newsitem.headline: Quaker Oats profit reverses loss despite weak Snapple.

text.p: Quaker Oats Co., still striving to turn around its struggling Snapple beverage unit, Thursday reported a profit for the fourth quarter, reversing a year-ago loss, but its earnings for the full year were off sharply.

Quaker said Snapple suffered an 8 percent decline in U.S. and Canadian sales in 1996, with volumes down 11 percent, as it continued to operate at a loss. However, sales of Diet Snapple increased 23 percent last year, it said.

Chicago-based Quaker said it earned $18.1 million, or 12 cents a share, in the fourth quarter, vs. a loss of $47.8 million, or 36 cents a share, in the 1995 period. Revenues in the latest quarter were $1.06 billion, down 10 percent from $1.18 billion a year earlier, which included $90.3 million from divested businesses.

The December 1995 quarter included a pretax restructuring charge of $40.8 million, or 18 cents per share, to reconfigure Snapple's manufacturing lines and to realign the company's European Beverages and Pacific Foods businesses.

For the full year, Quaker said it earned $244 million, or $1.80 a share, a 66 percent slide from the $720 million, or $5.39 per share it earned in 1995. Sales last year were $5.20 billion, 13 percent below the previous year's $5.95 billion, which included $796.9 million from divested businesses.
Quaker Chairman William Smithburg said Snapple "disappointed us with its lack of growth and operating loss.

"Our operating goals for Snapple in 1997 are to run the business at a cash profit, to achieve volume stability, and to bring a continuous flow of innovation and improved merchandising and distribution capabilities to this major brand," Smithburg said.
He said the six-flavor Diet Snapple line grew from 7 to 12 percent of Snapple's sales since its launch in January, 1996, and could grow to 25 percent in the future.
Outside of Snapple, Smithburg cited increased operating profits in other businesses.
"This was a rebound year in which our largest, value-driving businesses -- U.S. and Canadian Foods and Worldwide Gatorade -- increased their operating profits," said
He said major contributors were record operating income margins for the company's U.S. and Canadian Gatorade units and greatly improved margins for the U.S. and Canadian Foods businesses.

Smithburg cited Gatorade's continued profitable growth despite increased U.S. competition; strong volume growth in hot cereals and granola bars; broad-based gains in Canada and stronger operating profits for the company's Golden Grain, European Foods and Food Service units.

"One of our two biggest challenges was recouping the operating margin decline in ready-to-eat cereals following the price cut in June," Smithburg said in a statement accompanying the results. "Since then, we have outpaced the industry with two consecutive quarters of double-digit volume gains."
Smithburg said the company's hot cereals business had a strong year, with seven consecutive quarters of volume increases.

"We believe that consumer awareness of the recently approved FDA health claim, based on a petition submitted by Quaker, that 'soluble fiber from oatmeal, as part of a low saturated fat, low cholesterol diet, may reduce the risk of heart disease' should help keep that momentum going," he said.
Quaker's stock slipped 25 cents to $36.25 in midday trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
